claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Introducing a metastable high-entropy dual-phase microstructure can overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength.
The proposed intervention is the introduction of a metastable high-entropy dual-phase microstructure.
The resulting dual-phase microstructure consists of fcc and hcp phases.
Dislocation glide contributes to deformation of the proposed alloy.
Twinning contributes to deformation of the proposed alloy.
A phase transformation contributes to deformation of the proposed metastable alloy.
The intervention will increase both strength and ductility.
The intervention will improve fracture toughness.
Single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys are ductile but insufficiently strong.
The proposed intervention is applicable under room-temperature uniaxial tension.
The proposed material concept is applicable from room temperature to cryogenic temperatures.
The exact phase-transformation mechanism and its effect on mechanical properties are not fully understood.
Samples with different microstructures will be compared using uniaxial tensile testing.
Failure to increase both strength and ductility will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The starting material is already described as dual-phase, while the intervention is merely the introduction of a dual-phase microstructure. Metastability and fcc–hcp phase identity provide possible distinctions, but no concrete processing or compositional change explains how the initial dual-phase lamellae are converted.

The requested comparison is against the untreated eutectic dual-phase starting alloy, but the stated baseline is single-phase fcc HEAs. Consequently, the comparator for the predicted increase and the falsification rule is internally ambiguous.
